value.overview: The Tricolored Heron (Egretta tricolor) is a slender, medium-sized heron of the Americas. Its blue-gray body, white belly, and narrow white stripe down the front of the neck create a distinctive pattern. It usually hunts alone in shallow coastal and inland wetlands, often moving quickly through the water while chasing small fish. The species is also known as the Louisiana Heron and commonly nests in mixed colonies with other wading birds.
value.classification: The Tricolored Heron belongs to the heron family Ardeidae and the order Pelecaniformes. It is placed in the genus Egretta, which includes several slender herons and egrets.
value.identification: Adults are mostly slate blue or blue-gray above, with a white belly, white rump, and a long, narrow bill. A white line runs down the front of the dark neck. During breeding, adults may show buffy plumes on the back and warmer blue, purple, or orange tones on the neck and face. Immature birds are browner, especially on the neck and upperparts, and can resemble young Little Blue Herons but retain a contrasting pale belly.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from the southern United States through Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, and northern South America. In Costa Rica it is primarily found in the lowlands of both the Pacific and Caribbean slopes, especially around mangroves, estuaries, mudflats, coastal lagoons, marshes, river mouths, and other shallow wetlands. It is generally uncommon but widespread in suitable lowland habitat, and may occasionally occur at higher elevations, including parts of the Central Valley.
value.migrationStatus: Tricolored Herons from northern breeding populations migrate south in the nonbreeding season, while populations in Central and South America may be resident or locally mobile. In Costa Rica, it is mainly a winter resident and passage visitor, although some individuals may remain year-round and local breeding has been recorded, including on the Pacific side.
value.breeding: The Tricolored Heron usually nests colonially with other herons and egrets. It builds a platform of sticks in mangroves, shrubs, low trees, or dense wetland vegetation, often on islands or near coastal waters. Both adults help incubate the eggs and feed the young. Clutches commonly contain three or four eggs. In Costa Rica, breeding has been documented locally, including in coastal wetland areas, but the species is more often encountered there outside the main breeding season.
value.dietFeeding: Small fish make up most of the diet. The heron also takes shrimp, crabs, aquatic insects, frogs, lizards, and other small aquatic animals when available. It usually feeds in shallow water along marsh edges, mudflats, lagoons, mangroves, and estuaries. Its hunting style is active: it may walk, run, pause abruptly, spread its wings, or dart after prey before striking with its long bill.
value.behavior: This species is generally solitary while feeding, although it gathers with other wading birds at roosts and breeding colonies. It is mainly active during daylight and often returns to trees or mangroves to rest. Tricolored Herons are strong fliers, traveling with the neck folded back and the legs extended. Their quick, changeable movements while hunting are a useful field mark and distinguish them from slower, more deliberate herons.

conservation.populationTrend: The species remains widespread and globally secure, although available large-scale monitoring indicates an overall decline in recent decades and regional trends vary.
